items.title: Iodide n-factor is 2
items.description: States the iodide n-factor is 2 for the I⁻ → ICl conversion, recognizing a 2-electron oxidation from −1 to +1 rather than the 1-electron change to I₂.

provenance.evidence_detail: The mined pitfall 'Wrong iodide n-factor' identifies using n=1 (from I⁻/I₂ iodometry) as a high-severity error yielding 0.508 g/L, option (a).
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses n-factor = 1 for iodide, producing 0.508 g/L and selecting option (a).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key discriminative fact; sources caught 1/2 each, merged avoidance of I₂ assumption.

validation.gold_why: Uses ×2 for iodide in the equivalents equation.

items.title: Cerium n-factor is 1
items.description: States the n-factor of cerium is 1, corresponding to the one-electron reduction of Ce⁴⁺ in the titration.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts correctly identified Ce⁴⁺ → Ce³⁺ as a 1-electron change.
provenance.discriminates: A response that assigns n-factor = 2 to Ce⁴⁺, inflating equivalents and yielding 0.508 g/L.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Necessary for equivalents; caught 1/2 negatives, gold=FAIL so weighted moderately.

validation.gold_why: Uses normality directly; does not explicitly state Ce n-factor is 1.

items.title: Equivalents Ce = 0.001
items.description: Calculates the equivalents of cerium as 0.05 × 20/1000 = 0.001.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts computed 0.001 eq from N = 0.05 and V = 20 mL.
provenance.discriminates: A response that miscalculates equivalents (e.g., 0.002 from an inflated Ce n-factor or a decimal error).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required intermediate; caught 1/2 negatives, gold=pass.

validation.gold_why: Calculates (20 × 0.05)/1000 = 0.001 equivalents.

items.title: Moles iodide = 0.0005
items.description: Calculates the moles of iodide as 0.0005 mol by dividing 0.001 equivalents by the iodide n-factor of 2.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts computed 0.001 / 2 = 0.0005 mol of I⁻.
provenance.discriminates: A response that computes 0.001 mol (using n=1) or 0.000333 mol (using n=3).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Critical intermediate; caught 2/2 negatives, discrimination 1.00.

validation.gold_why: Does not explicitly state moles of iodide as 0.0005 mol.

provenance.calibration_rationale: Direct route to final answer; caught 2/2 negatives, gold=pass.

validation.gold_why: Explicitly states M_f = 1/500 M.

items.title: Mass iodide = 0.0635 g
items.description: Calculates the mass of iodide in the 250 mL sample as 0.0635 g (0.0005 mol × 127).

provenance.calibration_rationale: Key intermediate before g/L; caught 2/2 negatives, gold=FAIL so not weighted at 5.

validation.gold_why: Does not explicitly divide mass by 0.250 L; uses molarity approach instead.

items.title: Saddle-point condition
items.description: The saddle-point condition is stated as (p ± A(t_s))²/2 + I_p = 0, requiring the kinetic energy to equal −I_p and thereby forcing the complex saddle-point time t_s to be complex.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Missing I_p in saddle condition' (high severity): writing (p+A)²/2 = 0 instead of (p+A)²/2 + I_p = 0.
provenance.discriminates: A response that omits I_p from the saddle-point equation, leaving t_s real and losing all tunneling attenuation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core derivation step; caught 1/2 negatives. Forces complex time, load-bearing for the question.

validation.gold_why: Saddle-point condition with I_p not stated.

items.title: Complex time contour
items.description: The ionization amplitude is evaluated along a complex time contour that passes through the complex saddle-point time t_s in the lower or upper half-plane.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus that t_s must be complex and the action is evaluated along a complex time contour.
provenance.discriminates: A response that only integrates along the real time axis with no complex-time deformation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 1/2 negatives. Establishes the imaginary-time integration path central to the derivation.

validation.gold_why: Complex contour evaluation not described.

items.title: Static WKB exponent
items.description: In the static or quasistatic limit the ionization amplitude exponent is given as exp[−(2 I_p)^{3/2} / (3|E|)], with the factor 2^{3/2} present.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus static WKB amplitude exponent is M ~ exp[-(2 I_p)^{3/2} / (3|E|)].
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes I_p^{3/2}/(3|E|) or omits the factor 2^{3/2} from kinetic energy.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives. Canonical result; missing the 2^{3/2} factor is a common serious error.

validation.gold_why: Static WKB exponent not given.

items.title: Rate exponent doubled
items.description: The ionization rate W ~ |M|² carries the exponent exp[−2(2 I_p)^{3/2} / (3|E|)], differing by a factor of 2 from the amplitude exponent.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Amplitude vs rate exponent' (medium severity): reporting the amplitude exponent as the rate exponent without squaring.
provenance.discriminates: A response that quotes the same exponent for both the amplitude and the rate.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives. Distinguishing amplitude from rate exponent is a key intermediate distinction.

validation.gold_why: Rate exponent doubling not stated.

items.title: Static imaginary tunneling time
items.description: The static-limit imaginary tunneling time parameter is given as τ_s = √(2 I_p) / |E|, identified as the imaginary-time extent of the under-barrier segment.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus value τ_s = sqrt(2 I_p) / |E| for the static imaginary tunneling time.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives a different formula or no expression for the imaginary-time scale.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 1/2 negatives. Directly addresses the time-spent-under-barrier sub-question.

validation.gold_why: Static imaginary tunneling time not given.

items.title: Barrier exit coordinate
items.description: The static-limit barrier exit coordinate is given as z_exit = I_p / |E|, locating where the electron emerges in the continuum.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus barrier exit coordinate z_exit = I_p / |E|.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives an incorrect exit coordinate or conflates it with I_p^{3/2}/|E|.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives. Concrete intermediate result adding physical grounding to the tunneling picture.

validation.gold_why: Barrier exit coordinate not given.

provenance.discriminates: A response that confuses reducible inguinal hernia with communicating hydrocele despite the fluid-filled transillumination finding.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Plausible alternative diagnosis; caught 1/2 negatives, discrimination 0.50.

validation.gold_why: Does not diagnose inguinal hernia.

items.title: LLL projection stated
items.description: The response states that the single-particle theory projects electrons into the lowest Landau level, treating them as locked to the lowest quantum state of their circular motion.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) asks for a description of single-particle theory with electrons locked to the lowest quantum state of circular motion.
provenance.discriminates: A response that discusses general Landau levels without specifying lowest-Landau-level projection.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Zero discrimination but covers question premise; low weight for coverage only.

validation.gold_why: Reference does not mention LLL projection.

items.title: LLL degeneracy per area
items.description: The response states the lowest Landau level degeneracy per unit area as 1/(2π l_0²) or equivalently writes the filling factor ν = 2π l_0² n_e for the electrons.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct claims include LLL degeneracy 1/(2π l_0²) and filling factor relation ν = 2π l_0² n_e.
provenance.discriminates: A response that omits the macroscopic degeneracy, missing why partial filling matters.
provenance.calibration_rationale: 0.50 discrimination; core LLL quantity tying filling to density.

validation.gold_why: Reference is silent on degeneracy or filling factor.

items.title: Guiding center noncommutativity
items.description: The response states that the guiding center coordinates in the lowest Landau level are noncommuting, with [R_x, R_y] = ±i l_0², as a key feature of the single-particle theory.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct claim: guiding center coordinates are noncommuting, [R_x, R_y] = ±i l_0²; the sign is convention-dependent.
provenance.discriminates: A response treating guiding centers as ordinary commuting coordinates, missing the LLL algebra.
provenance.calibration_rationale: 0.50 discrimination; distinguishes LLL physics from ordinary gas.

validation.gold_why: Reference does not mention guiding center commutator.

items.title: Cyclotron energy frozen
items.description: The response states that the kinetic energy per electron in the lowest Landau level is frozen at E_0 = ℏω_c/2 = ℏ²/(2m l_0²).

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct claim: LLL projection freezes cyclotron motion at E_0 = ℏω_c/2.
provenance.discriminates: A response that assigns a continuous or dispersive kinetic energy to LLL electrons.
provenance.calibration_rationale: 1.00 discrimination; foundational quenching fact, all flawed responses missed it.

validation.gold_why: Reference does not mention cyclotron energy.

items.title: Kinetic energy is constant
items.description: The response states that after lowest-Landau-level projection the kinetic energy term in the field theory is H_kin = (ℏω_c/2) N_e, a pure number-operator constant with no spatial-gradient or dispersion term, avoiding forms such as (∇ψ)² or p²/2m at scales k ≪ l_0⁻¹.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) asks how the kinetic energy term appears in the field theory; consensus correct claim: H_kin = (ℏω_c/2) N_e with no gradient/dispersion term.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes a gradient kinetic term such as ∫ ψ*(−∇²)ψ in the LLL effective theory.
provenance.calibration_rationale: 1.00 discrimination; directly answers how kinetic term appears in EFT.

validation.gold_why: Reference does not discuss kinetic energy term.

items.title: LLL form factor as regulator
items.description: The response states that the projected density in the lowest Landau level carries the form factor F_0(q) = e^(−q²l_0²/4), which suppresses modes at q ~ l_0⁻¹ and provides a gauge-invariant UV regularization that is consistently regularized on the scale of l_0.

provenance.evidence_detail: Pitfall 'Regularization mechanism missing' (severity medium) and consensus claim that F_0(q) = e^(−q²l_0²/4) provides UV regularization.
provenance.discriminates: A response that merely asserts a cutoff at l_0 without connecting it to the LLL form factor.
provenance.calibration_rationale: 0.50 discrimination; addresses the regularization sub-question directly.

validation.gold_why: Reference does not mention form factor as regulator.

items.title: Interaction form factor correct
items.description: The response states that the interaction Hamiltonian for the partially filled lowest Landau level carries the form factor |F_0(q)|² = e^(−q²l_0²/2), writing H_int = (1/2)∫ d²q/(2π)² V(q) e^(−q²l_0²/2) ρ̄(q)ρ̄(−q), and avoids assigning e^(−q²l_0²/4) to the interaction vertex.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct claim: H_int = (1/2)∫ d²q/(2π)² V(q) e^(−q²l_0²/2) ρ̄(q)ρ̄(−q).
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses the single-particle form factor e^(−q²l_0²/4) in the interaction vertex.
provenance.calibration_rationale: 1.00 discrimination; all flawed responses used wrong form factor.

validation.gold_why: Reference does not give interaction Hamiltonian.

items.title: Interactions dominate partial fill
items.description: The response explicitly states that interactions dominate the behavior of the system when the lowest Landau level is not fully filled, because the kinetic energy is quenched to a constant and all nontrivial dynamics arise from interactions at scales k ≪ l_0⁻¹.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct claim: H_kin = (ℏω_c/2) N_e with no spatial gradient/dispersion term; all nontrivial dynamics come from interactions.
provenance.discriminates: A response that assigns residual single-particle dynamics to the LLL theory at long wavelengths.
provenance.calibration_rationale: 0.50–1.00 combined; matches reference answer, core conclusion.

validation.gold_why: Reference does not state dynamics come solely from interactions.

items.title: Quenched kinetic enables interactions
items.description: The response states that because the kinetic energy is quenched at partially filled filling, the lowest Landau level retains a macroscopic degeneracy that is lifted only by electron-electron interactions.

provenance.evidence_detail: Pitfall 'Interaction implications omitted' (severity high): the correct result states quenched kinetic energy leaves LLL states degenerate and interactions lift this degeneracy.
provenance.discriminates: A response that describes LLL projection but does not connect the quenched kinetic energy to the role of interactions.
provenance.calibration_rationale: 0.50 discrimination; key mechanistic link between quenching and interactions.

validation.gold_why: Reference does not mention quenched kinetic energy or degeneracy.

items.title: Force balance sphere A
items.description: Writes the force balance for sphere A as buoyant force d_F V g upward equals weight d_A V g downward plus tension T downward.

provenance.evidence_detail: All consensus rollouts wrote this per-sphere equation for sphere A; the system-only pitfall demonstrates it is load-bearing.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes only the combined-system equation cannot derive the individual density inequalities.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives; load-bearing derivation step, gold-fail so discounted.
provenance.merged_mirror_text: Writes the force balance for sphere B as buoyant force d_F V g upward plus tension T upward equals weight d_B V g downward.

validation.gold_why: Force balance for A not explicitly written.

items.title: Tension expression A
items.description: Derives the tension in the string on sphere A as T = (d_F − d_A) V g from the force balance.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus rollouts all derived this expression; the reversed-tension pitfall yields the wrong sign (d_A − d_F) instead.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes T = (d_A − d_F)Vg has reversed the tension direction and would select option (c).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives; key intermediate result enabling the density conditions.
provenance.merged_mirror_text: Derives the tension in the string on sphere B as T = (d_B − d_F) V g from the force balance.

validation.gold_why: Tension expression for A not derived.

items.title: Equate tensions
items.description: Sets the two tension expressions for the connected spheres equal, (d_F − d_A)Vg = (d_B − d_F)Vg, to derive d_A + d_B = 2d_F.

provenance.evidence_detail: All consensus rollouts performed this step; the not-equating-tensions pitfall shows omitting it drops option (d).
provenance.discriminates: A response that derives (a) and (b) but never equates the two T expressions will miss option (d).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives; critical algebraic step linking tensions to d_A+d_B=2d_F.

validation.gold_why: Tensions not equated explicitly.

items.title: Tension strictly positive
items.description: States that the tension T in the string is strictly positive (T > 0) because the arrangement specifies a taut string with nonzero tension.

provenance.evidence_detail: All consensus rollouts imposed T > 0; the dropping-T>0 pitfall shows that without it only option (d) survives.
provenance.discriminates: A response that allows T = 0 would accept d_A = d_F or d_B = d_F and fail to obtain the strict inequalities in options (a) and (b).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 1/2 negatives; bridges tension expressions to the density inequalities.

validation.gold_why: T > 0 not explicitly stated.

items.title: Derive d_A < d_F
items.description: Derives d_A < d_F from the condition that the tension expression T = (d_F − d_A)Vg is strictly positive for the immersed sphere A.

provenance.evidence_detail: All consensus rollouts connected T > 0 on sphere A to the inequality d_A < d_F; the dropping-T>0 pitfall targets this step.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states d_A < d_F as a guess without connecting it to T > 0 has not completed the required justification.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives; connects T>0 to selecting option (a).
provenance.merged_mirror_text: Derives d_B > d_F from the condition that the tension expression T = (d_B − d_F)Vg is strictly positive for the immersed sphere B.

validation.gold_why: d_A < d_F stated, not derived from tension.

items.title: Buoyant force formula
items.description: States that the buoyant force on each fully immersed sphere has magnitude d_F V g directed upward.

provenance.evidence_detail: All consensus rollouts used the buoyant force formula d_F·V·g; it is a load-bearing intermediate quantity for the force balances.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses a wrong buoyant force magnitude (e.g., d_A·V·g) would produce incorrect tension expressions.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives; foundational formula underlying the force balances.

validation.gold_why: Buoyant force formula not explicitly stated.

items.title: Average density insight
items.description: States that the relation d_A + d_B = 2d_F means the average density of the two solid spheres equals the fluid density d_F.

provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives; interpretive depth on the meaning of the density sum.

validation.gold_why: Average density insight not stated.

items.title: Independent-particle limitation
items.description: The response states that conventional band theory treats electrons as independent particles in a mean-field potential and therefore lacks the two-particle electron-hole correlation needed to predict excitons.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) target: band theory limitation due to independent-particle approximation and absence of two-particle correlation.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that vaguely says band theory is 'limited' without identifying the independent-particle / missing-correlation cause.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core explanation answering the question; caught 1/2 negatives with 0.50 discrimination.

validation.gold_why: Doesn't state independent-particle mean-field or two-particle correlation specifics.

items.title: Excitons as bound pairs
items.description: The response defines excitons as bound electron-hole pairs that are genuine two-particle correlated states absent from the single-particle band spectrum.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agree excitons are two-particle bound states below the gap, missing from independent-particle eigenstates.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that calls excitons merely 'excited conduction-band states' without the bound-pair / two-particle character.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Foundational definition; caught 1/2 negatives with 0.50 discrimination.

validation.gold_why: Doesn't define excitons as bound electron-hole pairs.

items.title: Band theory lacks excited states
items.description: The response states that conventional band theory does not account for correlated excited states such as excitons.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly says band theory 'does not account for excited states'; rollouts reframe this more technically but miss the direct statement.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that claims band theory predicts excited states and therefore should capture excitons.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Direct from reference answer; gold=pass, caught 1/2 negatives with 0.50 discrimination.

validation.gold_why: States band theory does not account for excited states.

items.title: Correlations produce attraction
items.description: The response identifies electron correlations as the physical mechanism that produces the attractive electron-hole interaction binding excitons, and states that conventional band theory ignores these correlations.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) target: role of electron correlations in creating attractive electron-hole interaction.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that attributes exciton absence to band theory being 'too simple' without naming electron correlations.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Central causal mechanism; caught 1/2 negatives with 0.50 discrimination; gold=FAIL but genuinely necessary.

validation.gold_why: Mentions correlations ignored but doesn't link to attractive e-h interaction.

items.title: Effective mass is kinematic only
items.description: The response states that the effective mass concept parametrizes band dispersion via the reduced mass μ and does not generate the Coulomb attraction that binds excitons.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Effective mass suffices' (severity high): conflating parametrization with binding mechanism.
provenance.discriminates: A response that says band theory plus effective masses yields excitons.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly answers question's effective-mass anchor; pitfall absorbed; caught 1/2 negatives, 0.50 discrimination.

validation.gold_why: Does not claim effective mass alone produces excitonic bound states.

items.title: On-site U contributes
items.description: The response states that the on-site Coulomb interaction U contributes to the formation of excitons.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly states on-site Coulomb interaction U plays 'a crucial role' in exciton formation.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that discusses mechanisms but never identifies on-site U as crucial to exciton formation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: From reference answer; gold=pass; caught 1/2 negatives with 0.50 discrimination.

validation.gold_why: States on-site Coulomb interaction U plays crucial role in formation.

items.title: U attractive in e-h channel
items.description: The response explains that the on-site Coulomb repulsion U, when viewed in the electron-hole channel, transmutes into an attractive interaction that binds localized Frenkel-type excitons rather than remaining repulsive as it is for two electrons.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Sign of U in e-h channel' (severity high): U transmutes to attraction under particle-hole transformation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims on-site U destabilizes or opposes exciton binding.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Highest discrimination (2/2, 1.00); pitfall absorbed into positive; key physics of U sign change.

validation.gold_why: Does not treat U as repulsive in e-h channel.

items.title: Screening renormalizes U
items.description: The response states that in realistic materials the on-site Coulomb interaction is screened to U_eff ≈ U/ε, where ε is the material dielectric constant.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agree screening renormalizes U_eff ~ U/ε and determines exciton character.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that uses bare unscreened U to set exciton binding energy in realistic materials.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Addresses realistic-materials sub-question; caught 1/2 negatives with 0.50 discrimination; pitfall absorbed.

validation.gold_why: Screening and U_eff not mentioned.

items.title: Screening sets exciton type
items.description: The response states that weak screening and large effective U yield tightly bound Frenkel excitons, while strong screening and small U yield Wannier-Mott excitons.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agree: weak screening + large U → Frenkel; strong screening + modest U → Wannier-Mott.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that discusses U but never connects screening strength to exciton type or localization.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives with 1.00 discrimination; connects U strength to exciton character in realistic materials.

validation.gold_why: Screening-related exciton types not mentioned.

items.title: Beyond-band-theory methods
items.description: The response names at least one beyond-conventional-band-theory method such as the Bethe-Salpeter equation or configuration interaction that includes the missing electron-hole interaction kernel.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts mention BSE and configuration interaction as methods including the electron-hole kernel.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that says correlations are needed but never identifies any formalism that supplies them.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds concrete remedy; caught 1/2 negatives with 0.50 discrimination; moderate importance.

validation.gold_why: No beyond-band-theory methods named.

items.title: Correlations vs mean-field
items.description: The response distinguishes electron correlations requiring explicit two-particle treatment from single-particle mean-field corrections such as Hartree-Fock exchange or DFT self-energies.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Correlations vs. exchange-only': exchange is mean-field, excitons need two-particle ladder diagrams.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that presents exchange or LDA corrections as sufficient for excitonic effects.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives with 1.00 discrimination; clarifies what does and does not count as correlation; pitfall absorbed.

validation.gold_why: No explicit distinction between correlations and mean-field corrections.

items.title: U in binding kernel
items.description: The response states that the on-site Coulomb interaction U enters the attractive direct term of the electron-hole interaction kernel, directly setting the exciton binding strength.

provenance.evidence_detail: Rollout 3 explicitly notes U enters the BSE kernel direct term; rollouts 1 and 2 omit this detail.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that discusses U only as a gap renormalization without its role in the binding kernel.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives with 1.00 discrimination but is a deeper detail; optional depth.

validation.gold_why: BSE kernel or binding kernel not mentioned.

items.title: Hydrogenic uses dielectric
items.description: The response states that the hydrogenic exciton binding formula uses the material dielectric constant ε in the Coulomb denominator, not the vacuum value ε = 1.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Unscreened hydrogenic formula' (severity medium): using ε = 1 gives binding energies orders of magnitude too large.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes the hydrogenic exciton formula with ε = 1 as if the solid were vacuum.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Real-materials detail; caught 1/2 negatives with 0.50 discrimination; adds concrete formula anchor.

validation.gold_why: Hydrogenic model and dielectric constant not mentioned.

items.title: Causal chain
items.description: The response provides a causal chain: conventional band theory ignores electron correlations, and because excitons require a correlated electron-hole attraction, they cannot appear in the single-particle spectrum.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) target requires a conceptual causal chain, not mere definitions.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that lists facts about band theory and excitons without connecting cause to effect.
provenance.calibration_rationale: gold=pass; caught 1/2 negatives; ties the argument together into the required conclusion.

validation.gold_why: Causal chain: ignores correlations → cannot predict excitons.

items.title: Reduced mass formula
items.description: The response states that the effective mass enters the exciton description through the reduced mass μ = m_e* m_h*/(m_e* + m_h*) in the hydrogenic model, and that the electron-hole Coulomb attraction must be added separately.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agree μ enters the hydrogenic model only after Coulomb attraction is externally added.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that mentions effective mass but never connects it to the hydrogenic reduced-mass parametrization.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific formula anchor for effective-mass sub-question; caught 1/2 negatives; adds precision.

validation.gold_why: Reduced mass and hydrogenic model not mentioned.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus across all rollouts and the reference that X and V factors explain chocolate agar growth.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives no growth factor explanation or cites wrong factors.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 1/2 negatives; mechanistic explanation linking the culture requirement to the organism's biology.

validation.gold_why: Mentions X and V growth factors in chocolate agar.

items.title: Factor X is hemin
items.description: The response identifies factor X as hemin, which is released from lysed red blood cells in chocolate agar.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Wrong growth factors cited' warns that X and V can be swapped.
provenance.discriminates: A response that labels factor X as NAD or swaps the two factor identities.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 1/2 negatives; adds biochemical specificity beyond the general X and V factor requirement.

validation.gold_why: Does not identify factor X as hemin.

items.title: Factor V is NAD
items.description: The response identifies factor V as NAD, which is also supplied by chocolate agar.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Wrong growth factors cited' warns that X and V can be swapped.
provenance.discriminates: A response that labels factor V as hemin.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 1/2 negatives; complementary biochemical detail to factor X identification.

validation.gold_why: Does not identify factor V as NAD.

items.title: Avoids N. meningitidis
items.description: The response avoids selecting Neisseria meningitidis as the causative agent, which would be a Gram-negative diplococcus growing on both chocolate and blood agar.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Confused with N. meningitidis' flagged as high severity.
provenance.discriminates: A response that answers Neisseria meningitidis based on age and meningitis alone.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives; the most common wrong organism based on overlapping pediatric meningitis presentation.

validation.gold_why: Does not select N. meningitidis.

items.title: Avoids reversed agar pattern
items.description: The response avoids reversing the culture results by claiming the organism grows on blood agar but not on chocolate agar.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Reversed agar growth pattern' flagged as high severity.
provenance.discriminates: A response that swaps the chocolate agar and blood agar growth findings.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 1/2 negatives; a specific factual error that inverts the defining culture characteristics.

validation.gold_why: Does not reverse agar growth pattern.

items.title: Stress urinary incontinence
items.description: Response names stress urinary incontinence as the condition most likely indicated by the described case.

provenance.evidence_detail: The single labelled sub-question asks for the most likely diagnosis; the reference answer and all consensus rollouts identify stress urinary incontinence.
provenance.discriminates: A response that diagnoses urge, overflow, or any other incontinence type.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core diagnosis; caught 2/2 negatives, discrimination 1.00.

validation.gold_why: Explicitly names stress urinary incontinence.

items.title: Triggers and abdominal pressure
items.description: Response states that the involuntary loss of urine occurs during physical activities that increase abdominal pressure, specifically naming coughing, laughing, lifting weight, or standing as triggers.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct claim that the triggers are activities increasing intra-abdominal pressure.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names the right condition but attributes leakage to detrusor contractions or spontaneous bladder emptying.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key mechanism link; merged sources caught 1/2 negatives each.

validation.gold_why: States leakage occurs during activities increasing abdominal pressure.

items.title: Multiparity to pelvic floor weakness
items.description: Response links the multiparous status or multiple pregnancies of this 40-year-old woman to pelvic floor muscle weakening.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct claim that multiparity with pelvic floor weakening is the key risk factor.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names stress urinary incontinence but does not explain why a multiparous woman is predisposed.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Identifies key risk factor; both sources caught 2/2 negatives, discrimination 1.00.

validation.gold_why: Links multiple pregnancies to pelvic floor weakening.

items.title: Weakened support and urethral closure
items.description: Response explains that weakened pelvic floor muscles reduce support for the bladder and urethra, causing the urethra to not stay completely closed when under increased abdominal pressure.

provenance.evidence_detail: The pitfall analysis correct_result states leakage occurs because weakened pelvic floor reduces urethral support, so increased intra-abdominal pressure exceeds urethral closure pressure.
provenance.discriminates: A response that describes the mechanism vaguely versus one that specifies the pressure dynamics causing leakage.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core pathophysiology; sources caught 2/2 negatives, discrimination 1.00.

validation.gold_why: Does not explicitly state pressure exceeds closure pressure.

items.title: Pelvic floor exercises
items.description: Response mentions pelvic floor exercises as a potential treatment option aimed at strengthening affected muscle groups.

provenance.calibration_rationale: Real treatment depth; caught 1/2 negatives, discrimination 0.50.

validation.gold_why: Mentions pelvic floor exercises as treatment.

items.title: Consult healthcare provider

provenance.discriminates: A response that provides no follow-up recommendation versus one that includes the provider consultation advice.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Appropriate guidance with limited discrimination; caught 1/2 negatives.

validation.gold_why: Advises consulting healthcare provider for treatment options.

items.title: Avoids urge misdiagnosis
items.description: Avoids identifying the condition as urge urinary incontinence, overactive bladder, or attributing the leakage to detrusor overactivity or bladder spasms instead of urethral sphincter insufficiency under increased abdominal pressure.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall of high severity: misdiagnosis as urge incontinence, confusing stress triggers with urgency symptoms.
provenance.discriminates: A response that diagnoses urge urinary incontinence, which would be wrong given the absence of urgency in the vignette.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common wrong diagnosis; sources caught 1/2 negatives, discrimination 0.50.

validation.gold_why: Does not identify condition as urge incontinence.

items.title: Avoids overflow misdiagnosis

provenance.discriminates: A response that diagnoses overflow incontinence, which requires retention or neurological features not present in the vignette.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific wrong diagnosis; caught 1/2 negatives, discrimination 0.50.

validation.gold_why: Does not state condition is overflow incontinence.

items.title: Absence of urgency supports stress
items.description: Response notes that the described symptoms do not include urgency, supporting stress urinary incontinence over urge urinary incontinence.

provenance.discriminates: A response that does not acknowledge the distinguishing features that exclude alternative diagnoses.

items.title: Breech body before head

items.title: Names extinction
items.description: The response identifies extinction as the psychological process that best explains why the 7-year-old patient stopped crying before physician visits.

provenance.evidence_detail: The single required deliverable is naming the psychological process; the reference and all rollouts identify extinction.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names habituation, counterconditioning, desensitization, or forgetting instead of extinction.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core answer; caught 2/2 negatives (disc 1.00). Correctness collapses without it.

validation.gold_why: Explicitly names extinction as the process.

items.title: Crying as conditioned response
items.description: The response states that the child's crying was a conditioned response developed through negative associations with prior medical experiences and that this response diminished through extinction.

provenance.evidence_detail: The consensus claim states: 'crying (CR)' is the conditioned response that diminishes during extinction.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names extinction but does not specify which behavior was the conditioned response.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Merges formation and diminishment of crying as CR; disc 0.50–1.00 across sources.

validation.gold_why: Identifies crying as the conditioned response.

items.title: Non-reinforced exposure mechanism
items.description: The response explains that extinction occurred because repeated physician visits no longer produced the expected negative outcome, weakening the conditioned association.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Unanswered mechanism linkage' (severity low) warns that a bare label 'extinction' without mapping to conditioning elements is insufficient.
provenance.discriminates: A response that provides only the bare label 'extinction' with no connection to the physician-visit scenario.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Mechanism applied to vignette; caught 2/2 negatives (disc 1.00) in both sources.

validation.gold_why: States child continued visits and negative outcome no longer occurred.

items.title: Extinction defined
items.description: The response defines extinction as the process by which a conditioned response diminishes because the expected negative outcome no longer occurs.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference states: 'Extinction occurs when the conditioned response, in this case, the crying, diminishes because the expected negative outcome no longer occurs.'
provenance.discriminates: A response that names extinction without stating what the process entails.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Formal definition distinct from mechanism; caught 2/2 negatives (disc 1.00).

validation.gold_why: Defines extinction as CR diminishing because expected outcome no longer occurs.

items.title: Association weakened over time
items.description: The response states that the association between physician visits and negative experiences weakened over time as the conditioned response diminished.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference states: 'Over time... this association weakened.'
provenance.discriminates: A response that states extinction occurred but does not describe the weakening of the prior association.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Captures temporal weakening of association; caught 2/2 negatives (disc 1.00).

validation.gold_why: States association weakened over time.

items.title: Visits became routine
items.description: The response states that physician visits became routine and devoid of negative experiences over time.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference states: 'as the visits became routine and devoid of negative experiences,' language no rollout used.
provenance.discriminates: A response that explains extinction mechanistically but omits the temporal/familiarity dimension of visits becoming routine.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key vignette detail enabling extinction; caught 2/2 negatives (disc 1.00).

validation.gold_why: States visits became routine and devoid of negative experiences.

items.title: Fear reduced
items.description: The response states that the child's fear of physician visits has been reduced, leading to the cessation of crying behavior.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference concludes: 'the child's fear of doctor visits has reduced, leading to the cessation of the crying behavior.'
provenance.discriminates: A response that identifies extinction but does not connect the process to the emotional outcome of reduced fear.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Connects emotional outcome to behavioral cessation; caught 1/2 negatives (disc 0.50).

validation.gold_why: States child's fear reduced, leading to cessation of crying.

items.title: CS identified as physician visit
items.description: The response identifies the physician visit as the conditioned stimulus that had been associated with negative medical experiences.

provenance.evidence_detail: The consensus claim states: 'physician visits (CS) associated with aversive medical experiences (US).'
provenance.discriminates: A response that names extinction but does not map the conditioning elements to the vignette.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Gold=FAIL but adds technical precision; kept low-weight for checklist completeness.

validation.gold_why: Does not explicitly use the term conditioned stimulus.

items.title: US identified as negative experience
items.description: The response identifies the prior negative medical experiences as the unconditioned stimulus that originally elicited crying.

provenance.evidence_detail: The consensus claim states: 'physician visits (CS) associated with aversive medical experiences (US), producing crying (CR).'
provenance.discriminates: A response that names extinction but does not specify what the original aversive stimulus was.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Gold=FAIL but caught 2/2 negatives; kept low-weight for technical depth.

validation.gold_why: Does not explicitly use the term unconditioned stimulus.

items.title: Avoids operant framing
items.description: Avoids framing the crying as an operant behavior reinforced by attention or escape, and instead identifies the process as classical extinction of a conditioned fear response.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Operant extinction confusion' warns that crying can be misread as an operant behavior maintained by attention.
provenance.discriminates: A response that labels the process as operant extinction or claims crying was previously reinforced by attention.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Observed trap; caught 2/2 negatives (disc 1.00), distinguishing classical from operant.

validation.gold_why: Frames as classical extinction, no operant framing present.

items.title: Avoids habituation label
items.description: Avoids naming habituation as the psychological process, instead identifying extinction as the weakening of the learned conditioned crying response.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Habituation vs extinction' (severity high) warns that habituation sounds plausible but applies to unconditioned responses, not learned fear associations.
provenance.discriminates: A response that answers 'habituation,' treating the diminished crying as a decreased innate response rather than weakening of a conditioned response.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Observed mislabel; caught 1/2 negatives (disc 0.50). Names correct process.

validation.gold_why: Does not mention habituation; names extinction.

items.title: Avoids counterconditioning label
items.description: Avoids naming counterconditioning as the psychological process, since the cessation occurred without the promise of rewards and without pairing the feared stimulus with a new positive association.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Counterconditioning claim' (severity high) warns that counterconditioning requires an active positive replacement, which the vignette rules out.
provenance.discriminates: A response that answers 'counterconditioning,' implying a new positive association was formed to replace the negative one.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Observed mislabel; caught 1/2 negatives (disc 0.50). Correctly excludes reward-based process.

validation.gold_why: Does not mention counterconditioning.

items.title: Names transference

provenance.calibration_rationale: Core concept; sources caught 1/2 and 1/2 negatives, proven signal.

validation.gold_why: Names transference as patient projecting feelings onto therapist.

items.title: Avoids countertransference label

provenance.discriminates: A response that uses the terms interchangeably or never clarifies the distinction.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Highest discrimination: caught 2/2 and 1/2 negatives; key directional distinction.

validation.gold_why: Does not explicitly mention countertransference or distinguish from it.

items.title: Positive or negative transference
items.description: The response notes that transference can involve positive or negative feelings projected onto the therapist, with the affectionate feelings in this case representing the positive pole.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference describes transference feelings as positive or negative, providing the affective context for the affectionate presentation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that implies transference is exclusively positive or exclusively negative.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/2 negatives; strong discriminative power for a key conceptual point.

validation.gold_why: Notes transference feelings can be positive or negative.

items.title: Misreads therapeutic empathy
items.description: The response states that the patient misinterprets the therapist's structured and empathetic attributes as signs of a personal emotional connection, characterizing this belief as an idealized distortion rather than a realistic appraisal.

provenance.evidence_detail: The 'Genuine rapport framing' pitfall is high severity; the reference explicitly frames the perception as mistaken and a distortion.
provenance.discriminates: A response that frames the patient's perception as accurate empathy or healthy therapeutic rapport.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly addresses the question's mistaken perception; 0/2 but covers core pitfall.

validation.gold_why: Describes misinterpretation as idealized distortion, not realistic appraisal.

items.title: Names idealization
items.description: The response identifies idealization as a mechanism alongside transference, describing the patient viewing the therapist as an exceptionally understanding figure.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts and the reference identify idealization as a specific subtype or mechanism operating in this scenario.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names only transference without identifying the idealization component.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Second primary mechanism in reference; key depth despite 0/2 measured negatives.

validation.gold_why: Identifies idealization as viewing therapist as exceptionally understanding.

items.title: EUPD vacillation cycle
items.description: The response notes that patients with emotionally unstable personality disorder vacillate between idealizing and devaluing important figures including therapists.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference states EUPD patients vacillate between idealizing and devaluing; no rollout mentioned this cycle.
provenance.discriminates: A response that presents a static, one-way idealization without the characteristic EUPD devaluation cycle.
provenance.calibration_rationale: EUPD-specific pattern from reference; anchors the diagnosis to the phenomenon.

validation.gold_why: States EUPD patients vacillate between idealizing and devaluing.

items.title: Avoids eroticized overlabel
items.description: Avoids upgrading the affectionate feelings described in the question to eroticized transference, which would imply sexual or romantic content the question does not describe.

provenance.evidence_detail: The 'Eroticized transference overlabel' pitfall is medium severity and was observed in rollout 1; the reference does not use the term eroticized.
provenance.discriminates: A response that labels the phenomenon as eroticized transference rather than positive/idealizing transference with affectionate feelings.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 1/2 negatives; specific overlabeling trap observed in flawed responses.

validation.gold_why: Does not upgrade to eroticized transference.

items.title: Craving for validation
items.description: The response identifies a deep craving for validation and support in EUPD patients as the underlying driver, where perceiving the therapist as empathetic affirms the patient's sense of being uniquely understood.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly names the craving for validation as the motivational engine; no rollout mentioned it.
provenance.discriminates: A response that explains the transference mechanism without identifying the validation-seeking motivation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Explains mechanism linking EUPD traits to the transference; merges two related points.

validation.gold_why: Identifies deep craving for validation and support in EUPD.

items.title: EUPD magnifies intensity
items.description: The response acknowledges that the emotional intensity and instability characteristic of emotionally unstable personality disorder magnify the effects of transference.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference states the intensity and instability of emotions in EUPD magnify transference effects, making the therapeutic process more complex.
provenance.discriminates: A response that describes transference generically without linking it specifically to EUPD's emotional intensity.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Connects diagnosis severity to phenomenon; low discrimination but real depth.

validation.gold_why: Notes EUPD intensity and instability magnify transference effects.

items.title: Maintain therapeutic boundaries

validation.gold_why: States therapist must maintain professional boundaries during exploration.

items.title: Combination of mechanisms

provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 1/2 negatives; synthesizes the two primary mechanisms into an integrated answer.

validation.gold_why: Describes combination of transference and idealization together.

validation.gold_why: Transference described as patient projecting onto therapist.

items.title: Energy formula stated
items.description: The response states the energy formula for the one-dimensional Ising model as E = -J Σ_n s_n s_{n+1} (or equivalent notation), where J is the coupling and the sum runs over sites along the chain.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) asks to derive the energy (Hamiltonian) formula; the reference gives E = -J Σ_n S_n S_{n+1}.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives a generic Hamiltonian without the specific nearest-neighbor Ising form.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core deliverable; caught 1/2 negatives, gold passed, highest importance.

validation.gold_why: E = -J Σ S_n S_{n+1} stated explicitly.

items.title: Negative sign before J
items.description: The energy formula for the Ising model contains a negative sign before the coupling J in the sum over nearest-neighbor spin products, so that E ∝ -J Σ s_i s_{i+1}.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Sign in Hamiltonian': writing E = +J Σ s_i s_{i+1} inverts ferromagnetic/antiferromagnetic behavior.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes E = +J Σ s_i s_{i+1}, making J>0 favor anti-aligned spins.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Sign is physics-critical; caught 1/2 negatives but overlaps with item 1.

validation.gold_why: Negative sign before J is present in formula.

items.title: Nearest-neighbor sum
items.description: The energy sum is explicitly restricted to nearest-neighbor pairs along the one-dimensional chain (e.g., Σ_n s_n s_{n+1} or Σ_{<i,j>}), not over all spin pairs.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Sum over wrong pairs': summing over all pairs or double-counting gives energy off by factor ~N.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes a sum over all pairs Σ_{i≠j} without restricting to nearest-neighbor bonds.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Nearest-neighbor restriction defines the model; caught 0/2 but gold passed, correctness-critical.

validation.gold_why: Sum uses S_n S_{n+1} nearest-neighbor pairs.

items.title: Boltzmann distribution
items.description: The response states that the probability of a configuration {S} is proportional to exp(-E({S})/(kT)) or equivalently exp(-βE) with a negative sign in the exponent.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Sign in Boltzmann exponent': writing e^{+E/kT} inverts the statistical mechanics relationship.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes P ∝ e^{+E/kT}, making high-energy states more probable.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Second core deliverable; caught 1/2 negatives, covers exponent sign pitfall.

validation.gold_why: Negative sign in exponent e^{-E/kT}.

items.title: Spins take values ±1
items.description: The response states or uses the convention that each spin variable at a site takes values s_i = ±1 (up or down), not {0, 1}.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Wrong spin values': using {0,1} instead of ±1 destroys the Ising algebra; all consensus rollouts state s_i = ±1.
provenance.discriminates: A response that defines spins as 0/1 or continuous variables.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Standard Ising convention; gold=FAIL and 0 discrimination, so low weight.

validation.gold_why: No mention that spins take values ±1.

items.title: J is interaction energy
items.description: The response identifies J as the interaction energy (coupling constant) between nearest-neighbor spins in the Ising model formula.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly states 'J is the interaction energy'.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives the formula but never defines what J represents.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Defines key parameter; 0 discrimination but gold passed and needed for correctness.

validation.gold_why: J is identified as interaction energy.

items.title: k is Boltzmann's constant
items.description: The response identifies k (or k_B) as Boltzmann's constant in the Boltzmann probability formula relating probability to energy.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer states 'k is Boltzmann's constant'.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes the Boltzmann formula but never defines k.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Symbol identification; 0 discrimination, low priority, reference-supported.

validation.gold_why: k identified as Boltzmann's constant.

items.title: T is temperature
items.description: The response identifies T as the temperature in the Boltzmann probability relation that connects energy to probability.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer states 'T is the temperature'.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives the Boltzmann formula but never defines T.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Symbol identification; 0 discrimination, low priority, reference-supported.

validation.gold_why: T identified as temperature.

items.title: Lower energy, higher probability
items.description: The response explains that configurations with lower energy have higher probability in the context of statistical mechanics, as a consequence of the Boltzmann distribution.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus item: all rollouts state that lower energy means exponentially larger Boltzmann weight, which is a key explanatory deliverable of sub-question (b).
provenance.discriminates: A response that states the formula P ∝ e^{-E/kT} but does not explain its physical meaning (lower E → higher P).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key conceptual link; caught 1/2 negatives, gold=FAIL but genuinely central to the question.

validation.gold_why: Does not explicitly explain lower energy gives higher probability.

items.title: Partition function normalization
items.description: The response mentions the partition function Z = Σ e^{-βE} as the normalizing constant for the probability of a configuration, or equivalently uses the proportionality symbol ∝.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Missing partition function': writing P = e^{-βE} as an equality without normalization gives probabilities that do not sum to 1.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes P({S}) = e^{-E/kT} as an equality without Z or ∝.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Proper normalization; caught 1/2 negatives, real added depth beyond bare formula.

validation.gold_why: Uses proportionality symbol ∝ for Boltzmann relation.

items.title: Beta correctly defined
items.description: If the response uses β in the Boltzmann formula, it defines β = 1/(k_B T) where k is Boltzmann's constant and T is temperature, rather than β = k_B T.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Inverted β definition': defining β = k_B T instead of 1/(k_B T) inverts the temperature dependence.
provenance.discriminates: A response that defines β = kT, making higher temperature sharpen the distribution on low energy.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Prevents inverted-β error; 0 discrimination but correctness-critical if β is used.

validation.gold_why: β not used; condition is vacuously satisfied.

items.title: External field convention
items.description: The response states whether an external magnetic field term (-h Σ s_i) is included or deliberately omitted in the Ising energy formula for the one-dimensional model.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Unstated external field': the question does not mention a field, making the convention ambiguous if not stated.
provenance.discriminates: A response that silently includes or omits the field term without acknowledging the choice.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Clarifies scope; caught 1/2 negatives, gold=FAIL, genuine but secondary depth.

validation.gold_why: No mention of external field term.

items.title: Spins on one-dimensional chain
items.description: The response conveys that spins are arranged on a one-dimensional chain (lattice) with nearest-neighbor interactions between adjacent sites.

provenance.evidence_detail: The question structure specifies a one-dimensional lattice with nearest-neighbor interactions; the derivation must reflect this geometry.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives a 2D or mean-field Ising formula without addressing the 1D chain structure.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Establishes model geometry; 0 discrimination but anchors the one-dimensional constraint.

validation.gold_why: States one-dimensional model with S_n S_{n+1}.

items.title: Derivation from pair interactions
items.description: The response explains that the total energy is obtained by summing nearest-neighbor bond energies -J s_i s_{i+1} over all adjacent pairs in the one-dimensional chain.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus item: bond energy sign convention and summation over bonds; the question asks to 'derive' not just state.
provenance.discriminates: A response that merely writes the final formula without any derivation step from individual bond energies.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Shows derivation logic; caught 1/2 negatives, gold=FAIL, real but supplementary.

validation.gold_why: No derivation explaining summation of bond energies.

items.title: Configuration notation
items.description: The response uses a configuration notation such as {S} or {s_i} to label a complete spin configuration in both the energy and probability expressions.

provenance.discriminates: A response that writes E and P without connecting them through a shared configuration label.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Notational clarity; 0 discrimination, minor added value for completeness.

validation.gold_why: Uses {S} notation for configuration.

items.title: GPI anchor deficiency
items.description: Identifies a deficiency of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor as the underlying molecular defect in this presentation.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts diagnosed SLE and proposed defective apoptotic debris clearance; the reference identifies GPI anchor deficiency as the molecular defect.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names SLE or immune complex deposition but never mentions the GPI anchor.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives with 1.00 discrimination; central molecular defect without which the answer is wrong.

validation.gold_why: Explicitly identifies GPI anchor deficiency as the molecular defect.

items.title: GPI anchor attachment role
items.description: States that the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor is necessary for the attachment of protective proteins to the cell surface.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference describes GPI anchor as necessary for attachment of various protective proteins to the cell surface.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions CD55 or CD59 without explaining that they require the GPI anchor for surface attachment.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; explains why GPI deficiency matters mechanistically but is secondary to naming the defect.

validation.gold_why: States GPI anchor necessary for attachment of protective proteins.

items.title: CD55 and CD59 lost
items.description: Names CD55 and CD59 as the specific glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored complement regulatory proteins lost from the cell surface.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly names CD55 and CD59; no rollout mentioned either protein.
provenance.discriminates: A response that discusses complement regulation but omits the specific surface protectins CD55 and CD59.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives with 1.00 discrimination; the two proteins are the concrete entities the question targets.

validation.gold_why: Names CD55 and CD59 as missing GPI-anchored proteins.

items.title: Complement regulation failure
items.description: States that the impaired immunological process is failure to regulate complement activity on the surface of blood cells.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference concludes that the impaired process is the failure to regulate complement on blood cell surfaces due to absent GPI-anchored protective proteins.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names a different impaired process such as defective apoptotic debris clearance or type III hypersensitivity.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; directly answers the question's ask for the specific impaired process.

validation.gold_why: States failure to regulate complement on blood cell surfaces.

items.title: Uncontrolled complement activation
items.description: States that loss of CD55 and CD59 leads to uncontrolled complement activation on blood cells.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts attributed complement activation to immune complex deposition (classical pathway); the reference attributes it to loss of complement regulation by CD55 and CD59.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions complement but frames it as immune complex–triggered rather than unregulated due to missing protectins.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; key mechanistic link between protein loss and cell destruction.

validation.gold_why: States loss leads to uncontrolled complement activation on cell surfaces.

items.title: RBCs susceptible to lysis
items.description: States that absence of GPI-anchored protective proteins makes red blood cells susceptible to complement-mediated destruction.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference states that lack of GPI-anchored proteins such as CD55 and CD59 on red blood cells makes them susceptible to uncontrolled complement activation and subsequent destruction.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names CD55 and CD59 but does not explain that their absence renders RBCs susceptible to complement lysis.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; connects the molecular defect to the downstream cellular consequence.

validation.gold_why: States absence makes RBCs susceptible to complement-mediated destruction.

items.title: Intravascular hemolysis
items.description: Identifies intravascular hemolysis as the consequence of complement-mediated destruction of red blood cells.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly states that uncontrolled complement activation causes intravascular hemolysis; no rollout identified this mechanism.
provenance.discriminates: A response that explains cytopenias via bone marrow failure or immune complex nephritis rather than complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; the specific type of hemolysis is critical for explaining the clinical findings.

validation.gold_why: Identifies intravascular hemolysis as consequence of complement destruction.

items.title: Hemolytic anemia correlation
items.description: States that complement-mediated destruction of red blood cells produces hemolytic anemia manifested as tea-colored urine.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly connects hemolytic anemia to the tea-colored urine presentation due to hemoglobinuria.
provenance.discriminates: A response that separates the anemia from the urinary finding or explains them through different mechanisms.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; links the mechanism to the observed anemia and urine finding.

validation.gold_why: States complement-mediated RBC destruction causes hemolytic anemia with tea-colored urine.

items.title: Hemoglobinuria from hemolysis
items.description: Attributes the tea-colored urine to hemoglobinuria resulting from intravascular hemolysis.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts interpreted tea-colored urine as glomerular hematuria from lupus nephritis; the reference explains it as hemoglobinuria from complement-mediated RBC destruction.
provenance.discriminates: A response that attributes tea-colored urine to glomerular bleeding or nephritis rather than hemoglobinuria.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; distinguishes hemoglobinuria from hematuria, a key diagnostic point.

validation.gold_why: Attributes tea-colored urine to hemoglobinuria from intravascular hemolysis.

items.title: PNH diagnosis
items.description: Identifies the clinical diagnosis as Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH).

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts diagnosed SLE; the reference identifies PNH as the associated diagnosis.
provenance.discriminates: A response that diagnoses SLE or lupus nephritis instead of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; diagnostic framing that contextualizes the mechanism, though the question asks for process not diagnosis.

validation.gold_why: Identifies PNH as the clinical diagnosis.

items.title: Cytopenias linked to mechanism

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference states that the PNH process can contribute to the observed cytopenias including anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia.

provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; ties the peripheral cytopenias to the underlying process rather than leaving them unexplained.

validation.gold_why: Links cytopenias to PNH and complement dysregulation mechanism.

items.title: Avoids SLE diagnosis
items.description: Avoids attributing this presentation to systemic lupus erythematosus with defective clearance of apoptotic debris and immune complexes rather than to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts diagnosed SLE with defective apoptotic debris clearance; the reference diagnoses PNH with GPI anchor deficiency.

provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; SLE is the primary competing diagnosis given cytopenias in a young female.

validation.gold_why: No mention of SLE; attributes presentation to complement-mediated hemolysis.

items.title: Avoids hematuria interpretation

provenance.evidence_detail: The mined pitfall 'Hematuria vs hemoglobinuria' notes that all rollouts read tea-colored urine as nephritic hematuria rather than hemoglobinuria.
provenance.discriminates: A response that interprets dark urine as renal immune complex deposition rather than hemoglobinuria from intravascular hemolysis.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; misreading hemoglobinuria as hematuria leads to wrong workup and wrong mechanism.

validation.gold_why: Attributes urine to hemoglobinuria, not glomerular hematuria or lupus nephritis.

items.title: Avoids type III/classical pathway
items.description: Avoids naming type III hypersensitivity or classical complement pathway activation via immune complex deposition as the specific impaired immunological process.

provenance.evidence_detail: The mined pitfall 'Wrong complement mechanism' identifies type III hypersensitivity as the wrong mechanism chosen once SLE is assumed.
provenance.discriminates: A response that selects type III hypersensitivity and immune complex deposition instead of complement dysregulation from GPI anchor deficiency.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; the SLE framing naturally leads to this wrong mechanism, a shared error.

validation.gold_why: No mention of type III hypersensitivity.

items.title: Contrasts Inhibitor vs Inducers

items.title: OCs Are Active Drugs
items.description: The response indicates that oral contraceptives are active drugs whose levels are not reduced by CYP450 inhibition because they do not require metabolic activation.

items.title: Selects option A
items.description: The response selects option A, identifying efferent arteriole constriction as the mechanism of action.

items.title: Glomerular pressure rises

items.title: Filtration fraction formula
items.description: The response states that filtration fraction equals GFR divided by renal plasma flow.

items.title: Renal plasma flow

items.title: FF rises via GFR
items.description: The response states that filtration fraction increases because GFR rises under efferent arteriole constriction.

provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 1/2 negatives; links GFR increase to filtration fraction rise, partial mechanism explanation.

items.title: Afferent lowers pressure

items.title: Renal artery lowers GFR

provenance.calibration_rationale: Merged item caught 1/2 from content; rules out option B; gold=FAIL so low weight.

validation.gold_why: Renal artery constriction effect not discussed.

items.title: Efferent dilation lowers pressure

validation.gold_why: Efferent dilation effect not discussed.

items.title: Permeability excluded
items.description: The response states that peritubular capillary permeability changes do not selectively increase GFR and filtration fraction.

items.title: Avoids FF sign error
items.description: The response avoids reasoning that decreased renal plasma flow causes filtration fraction to decrease under efferent arteriole constriction.

validation.gold_why: No incorrect FF sign reasoning present.

items.title: Avoids single-variable FF
items.description: The response avoids concluding that any GFR increase raises filtration fraction.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'RPF omitted from FF': reasoning only about GFR when evaluating FF, forgetting the ratio requires RPF.

items.title: Treatment may be effective

items.title: Notes small sample size
items.description: The response notes the small sample size of 5 patients as a limitation affecting the interpretation of the test results.

items.title: Fails to reject null
items.description: The response states that the null hypothesis is not rejected because the p-value is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level.

items.title: Compares p to 0.05
items.description: The response explicitly compares the p-value 0.050059 to the 0.05 threshold and notes it is above 0.05.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Boundary p-value misclassification' notes the temptation to round 0.050059 to 0.05.
provenance.discriminates: Catches responses that round p = 0.050059 down to 0.05 and declare significance.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; the marginal exceedance is the central reasoning step.

items.title: Uses paired t-test
items.description: The response identifies the paired t-test as the test used for the before-and-after scores from the same patients.

items.title: States critical t 2.776
items.description: The response states the two-tailed critical t-value of 2.776 at α = 0.05 with df = 4 for the test on patients.

items.title: Links p-value to power
items.description: The response connects the marginal p-value of 0.050059 to the low statistical power inherent in a sample size of 5 patients.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference ties the small sample size and the p-value together; rollouts never made this connection.
provenance.discriminates: Catches responses that treat the p-value and sample size as separate unrelated facts.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 3/3 negatives; power reasoning explains why significance was missed.

validation.gold_why: Does not mention statistical power.

items.title: Identifies df = 4
items.description: The response identifies the degrees of freedom as 4 for the paired t-test with 5 patients and their before and after scores.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agreed df = 4 for n = 5; this is consistent with the paired t-test.
provenance.discriminates: Catches responses that use incorrect degrees of freedom.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Gold=FAIL, 0/3 caught; intermediate quantity kept for coverage at low weight.

validation.gold_why: Does not mention degrees of freedom.

items.title: Avoids one-tailed test
items.description: Avoids using a one-tailed test with hypothesis H1: μ_d > 0 or critical t = 2.132, and instead uses a two-tailed test.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'One-tailed vs two-tailed'; rollout 3 committed to one-tailed with t = 2.132.
provenance.discriminates: Catches responses that use a one-tailed test because 'improving' sounds directional.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Caught 2/3 negatives; one-tailed analysis yields the wrong p-value.

validation.gold_why: Uses two-tailed test, no one-tailed commitment.

items.title: Avoids Wilcoxon as primary
items.description: Avoids presenting the Wilcoxon signed-rank test as the primary test instead of the paired t-test that yields the p-value for these patients.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Wilcoxon vs t-test mismatch'; with n = 5, switching to non-parametric is tempting but the reference uses the paired t-test.
provenance.discriminates: Catches responses that default to Wilcoxon signed-rank and produce a different p-value.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Gold=pass, 0/3 caught; real methodological pitfall kept at minimum weight.

validation.gold_why: No mention of Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
